question.text: Hypothetical Scenario (for Five Forces framework practice): Sunita Reddy, a research analyst at Alpha Research, is applying Porter's Five Forces framework to an illustrative commodity-manufacturing industry. The caselet's industry facts are hypothetical and used only to exercise the framework: (1) The industry has 50+ players with the top 5 controlling 45% market share, and the product is a homogeneous commodity. (2) Key raw materials are sourced from a limited number of suppliers, and government controls input licences. (3) Demand is driven by construction-linked end-use, with large institutional buyers purchasing in bulk. (4) A new plant requires very high upfront investment plus regulatory clearances. (5) Substitute construction materials are gaining share in some urban segments, and industry EBITDA margins sit in the mid-teens. Question 2 of 5: The bargaining power of suppliers in this hypothetical industry is:

answer.text: Low because there are thousands of suppliers
Moderate to High because the number of suppliers is limited and government controls licences for critical inputs
Non-existent because manufacturers own all input sources
Low because the key raw material is freely available everywhere

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook says supplier power is high when the number of suppliers is limited and they supply critical inputs, and treats licensing/permissions as an entry-barrier factor. A limited supplier base combined with government-controlled input licences gives those suppliers leverage over manufacturers that depend on the critical input. The Trap: Assuming all manufacturers are vertically integrated removes the supplier force by assumption rather than analysis. Even where some firms own input sources, the rest of the industry still faces concentrated suppliers. Note: The industry facts in this caselet are hypothetical and chosen to illustrate the supplier-power force; they should not be read as describing any specific real-world industry.
